## TL;DR

Wired Apple notarization, ticket stapling, and post-staple verification into the
existing `release` job in `.github/workflows/macos-hub.yml`. The signed
`RepoOSHub.dmg` is now submitted after packaging and the DMG install-experience
check and before any GitHub Release upload. A rejected submission or wait
timeout fails the job and, when Apple returned a submission ID, fetches
`notarytool log` with the same authentication options so the reason appears in
CI. Only an `Accepted` submission reaches `stapler staple`,
`stapler validate`, and `spctl --assess`; the upload step runs only after every
gate passes. A new `dry_run` `workflow_dispatch` input exercises the whole
pipeline without creating or modifying a release. `docs/macos-hub-release.md`
no longer describes the DMG as ad-hoc signed or a Gatekeeper warning as
expected, and now documents the secret set, the gate order, the dry run, the
release checklist, and failure triage.

I validated the workflow's shell branches locally with stubbed `xcrun`,
`spctl`, and submission JSON (missing credentials, accepted, rejected, timeout,
and failure before an ID). I did not run a real Apple submission: that requires
the #0578 Developer ID signing work and the #0576 credentials, neither of which
is available in this worktree.

## Work and rationale

The release job already built the app, packaged `RepoOSHub.dmg`, and verified
the DMG install experience. I inserted one step, `Notarize, staple and verify
DMG`, between that check and `Determine channel`/`Upload DMG to GitHub Release`.
Keeping it in the existing job preserves the exact artifact that was checked.

I used one step rather than separate submit/log/staple steps because the
authentication arguments must be identical for submission and log retrieval.
Building the `AUTH_ARGS` array once keeps the ID, status, credentials, and trap
cleanup in one shell scope. It also guarantees that a failure path cannot
accidentally reach stapling, because the step exits first.

Credential selection follows the runbook's existing contract exactly: if any of
`APPLE_API_KEY`, `APPLE_API_KEY_ID`, or `APPLE_API_ISSUER_ID` is present, all
three are required and the API-key path wins; otherwise `APPLE_ID`,
`APPLE_APP_SPECIFIC_PASSWORD`, and `APPLE_TEAM_ID` are required. An incomplete
set fails immediately with a message naming the missing variables. The API
`.p8` is written only in `$RUNNER_TEMP`, chmodded, and removed in a trap, so it
survives neither success nor failure. No secret value is echoed.

Submission pipes through `tee` into `$RUNNER_TEMP/notarytool-submit.json` under
`set -euo pipefail`, then parses `id` and `status` with `jq`. If no ID came
back, the step prints whatever output exists, reports that no Apple log is
available, and exits with the original nonzero status. If an ID exists but the
status is not `Accepted` or the exit code is nonzero, it prints the ID, fetches
`notarytool log "$ID"` with the same `AUTH_ARGS`, and exits nonzero. The ID and
status also go to the job summary for diagnostics.

Stapling is deliberately downstream of the accepted check. `stapler staple`,
`stapler validate`, and `spctl --assess --type open --context
context:primary-signature` run as plain commands under `set -e`, so each is a
fatal gate with no `|| true` or post-stapling fallback.

The upload step now has `if: ${{ inputs.dry_run != 'true' }}`. A tag push has no
`dry_run` input, so it uploads as before; a manual dry run skips only the
upload, not notarization. I used a string comparison because `workflow_dispatch`
inputs can reach expressions as strings even when declared boolean, and a
comparison against the boolean `true` could silently fail open for a `"true"`
string.

The runbook had actively contradictory statements: it called the DMG ad-hoc
signed and not notarized, and told maintainers a Gatekeeper warning was
expected. I replaced those with the real contract: submission, wait, log on
failure, staple, validate, assess, then upload. I documented the repository
Actions secret names the job reads, the API-key/app-password precedence, the
exact gate sequence, the `dry_run` path and its prerequisites, a checklist item
for successful notarization and stapling, and triage for rejection, timeout,
post-submission file drift, and incomplete secrets.

## Approaches tried

I considered separate "Submit", "Fetch log on failure", "Staple", and "Verify"
steps sharing the ID through `GITHUB_OUTPUT`. That is more readable in the
Actions UI, but it would duplicate credential resolution (or require a second
authentication path) and make "same authentication options" a convention rather
than a guarantee. The single step keeps the contract enforceable.

I also considered moving the logic into `macos/scripts/` so it could be tested
directly. I rejected that because the acceptance criteria point at the workflow
itself, an extra script adds a new execution surface, and the logic is short
enough to audit inline. For local validation I extracted the `run:` block,
syntax-checked it with `bash -n`, and exercised it against fake `xcrun` and
`spctl` binaries plus real `jq`. That covered the branches that matter without
needing Apple credentials.

For the dry-run switch I considered checking secrets in the upload step's `if:`.
GitHub does not make secret values reliably available to `if:` expressions, and
the requirement is to fail before upload rather than skip. Shell validation in
the notarization step is therefore the right gate: missing credentials fail the
job loudly, and the upload never becomes a fallback.

## Challenges and blockers

The main blocker is the dependency chain. #0577 (hardened runtime/entitlements)
and #0578 (Developer ID signing) are still inbox, so the release job currently
builds an artifact that cannot pass notarization. That is intentional
fail-closed behavior for this task, not a hidden regression: the acceptance
criteria require the gate, and an unsigned or invalidly signed DMG must never
be uploaded. End-to-end proof needs #0578 plus maintainer-provisioned #0576
secrets; it cannot be produced from this worktree, and I have not claimed it.

A practical friction point was `repoos check`: it created a WIP checkpoint
mid-run and left the edited files read-only, so a follow-up one-line workflow
edit initially failed. I restored write permission, reapplied the change, and
planned a final scoped run on the settled tree. I also had to be careful that
the boolean/string comparison in the upload condition could not fail open in a
dry run.

## Key learnings

- Notarization failure handling is a two-phase problem: rejections and timeouts
  can return an ID, while invalid signatures may fail before any ID exists.
  Both paths need distinct, honest diagnostics.
- `tee` without `pipefail` would mask a rejected submission; the pipeline status
  must come from `notarytool`.
- Stapling must be unreachable unless the status is exactly `Accepted`; a
  successful exit code alone is not the acceptance check.
- A dry run is a test of the gate, not an override: it must still require real
  signing and notarization credentials and must never create or modify a
  release.
- The repository already had one authoritative secret contract in the runbook;
  the workflow and docs are safer when they quote the same names and order
  rather than inventing a second variant.
